common.sentence: Lea erklärt dem neuen Mitglied die Probenordnung des Chors.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of erklärt; des Chors identifies the group whose rules are explained.

common.sentence: Der Chorvorstand erinnert alle an die Anmeldefrist für das Probenwochenende.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular after an in jemanden an etwas erinnern; für identifies the event.

common.sentence: Ben organisiert Fahrgemeinschaften für den Chor zum Auftritt im Nachbarort.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative plural object of organisiert; zum Auftritt identifies the destination event.

common.sentence: Für das Chorfest übernimmt Mara den Schichtplan am Getränkestand.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of übernimmt; am Getränkestand identifies where the shifts take place.

common.sentence: Lea fragt nach einer Ablösung am Stand, damit Ben Pause machen kann.

language_specific.grammar: Dative singular after nach in nach etwas fragen; here the noun refers to someone taking over a duty.

common.sentence: Der Chor bittet das Publikum um eine freiwillige Eintrittsspende für den Saal.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular after um in um etwas bitten; freiwillige makes the contribution voluntary.

common.sentence: Ben verteilt beim Chorfest Mehrwegbecher und sammelt sie später wieder ein.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative plural object of verteilt; sie refers back to the cups.

common.sentence: Die Kassenwartin zählt das Wechselgeld für den Getränkestand beim Chorfest.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of zählt; the money is kept ready to give customers change.

common.sentence: Bei der Chorversammlung stellt Mara einen Änderungsantrag zum vorgeschlagenen Konzerttermin.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular in einen Änderungsantrag stellen; zum identifies the proposal to be amended.

common.sentence: Der Chorvorstand prüft die Beschlussfähigkeit vor der Wahl der Kassenwartin.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of prüft; vor der Wahl places the check before the election.

common.sentence: Lea liest das Ergebnis der geheimen Wahl des Chorvorstands vor.

language_specific.grammar: Genitive singular after Ergebnis; geheimen has the weak ending after der.

common.sentence: Im Nachbarschaftschor singt Mara die zweite Stimme zur Melodie.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of singt; zweite has a weak ending after die. Zur Melodie identifies the part's relationship to the melody.

common.sentence: Die Chorleiterin lässt den Sopran die Melodie allein singen.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular with lässt singen; here Sopran refers collectively to the choir's soprano singers.

common.sentence: Bei der Chorprobe hält Ben den Grundton des Akkords.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of hält; des Akkords identifies the chord whose root Ben sustains.

common.sentence: Die Chorleiterin erklärt den Auftakt und zeigt danach den Dreiertakt.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of zeigt; Dreiertakt denotes a meter with three beats per measure.

common.sentence: Vor dem Konzert übt der Chor das Stück a cappella.

language_specific.usage: In this choir context, the phrase specifies singing without instrumental accompaniment.

common.sentence: Lea markiert den Bindebogen über den drei verschiedenen Noten.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of markiert; the slur joins notes to be performed as a connected phrase.

common.sentence: Der Chor singt die erste Strophe leise und die zweite kräftig.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of singt; die zweite refers to a second verse.

common.sentence: Der Klavierbegleiter notiert den Fingersatz für die Klavierstelle in seinen Noten.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of notiert; für die Klavierstelle identifies the passage for which the finger positions are written.

common.sentence: Beim Proben des Liedes spricht der Chor zuerst den Text im Rhythmus.

language_specific.grammar: Dative singular after im, contracted from in dem; im Rhythmus sprechen means to speak in time with the rhythm.

common.sentence: Die Chorleiterin lässt den letzten Ton ohne Vibrato singen.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular after ohne; Vibrato denotes a slight, regular variation in pitch.

common.sentence: Für die neue Sängerin sucht Lea einen Platz im Alt.

language_specific.grammar: Dative singular after im, contracted from in dem; here Alt names the choir's alto section.

common.sentence: Ben prüft, ob das Klavier für die Chorprobe gestimmt ist.

language_specific.grammar: Gestimmt forms a state passive with ist; the sense is tuning an instrument.

common.sentence: Für den Probenraum braucht der Chor noch einen Schlüsselbund.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of braucht; für den Probenraum identifies the room for which the keys are needed.

common.sentence: Lea hängt den Probenkalender im Eingang des Nachbarschaftshauses auf.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of hängt auf; the calendar lists rehearsal dates.

common.sentence: Beim Chorfest übernimmt Mara die Kuchenausgabe am Buffet.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of übernimmt; am Buffet identifies where the cake is served.

common.sentence: Der Chorvorstand sucht eine Vertretung für die erkrankte Chorleiterin.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of sucht; für identifies the person for whom a substitute is needed.

common.sentence: Bei der Vorstandswahl im Nachbarschaftschor verteilt Lea die Stimmzettel.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative plural object of verteilt; the ballot papers are for the choir's board election.

common.sentence: Der Chor bestimmt zwei Personen als Wahlvorstand für die Vorstandswahl.

language_specific.grammar: Singular noun after als, identifying the role assigned to the two people; the Wahlvorstand conducts the election.

common.sentence: Nach der Probe legt Ben die Fundsachen auf den Tisch.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative plural object of legt; Fundsachen are items that have been found.

common.sentence: Zum Jubiläum des Chors gestaltet Mara eine Fotowand mit alten Probenbildern.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of gestaltet; mit identifies the photographs used in the display.

common.sentence: Mara zu ihrer Chorfreundin Lea: „Ich ziehe um; erzähl das bitte nicht weiter.“

language_specific.grammar: Weiter closes the imperative verb bracket; das refers to Mara's news that she is moving.
language_specific.usage: Mara asks her choir friend not to pass on her news.

common.sentence: Lea zu ihrer Chorfreundin Mara: „Ich bin für dich da, wenn du mich brauchst.“

language_specific.grammar: Bin is first-person singular; für governs accusative dich, and da completes the predicate.
language_specific.usage: Lea offers her choir friend continuing support when needed.

common.sentence: Ben zu seiner Chorfreundin Mara: „Das bleibt unter uns, versprochen.“

language_specific.grammar: Unter governs dative uns in this fixed phrase.
language_specific.usage: Ben promises his friend that the matter will remain confidential.

common.sentence: Lea zu ihrem Chorfreund Ben: „Mein Gehalt geht dich nichts an.“

language_specific.grammar: Dich is accusative; an closes the verb bracket. Nichts is part of the fixed negative expression.
language_specific.usage: Lea firmly tells her choir friend that her salary is private; the wording can sound abrupt.

common.sentence: Mara zu ihrer Chorfreundin Lea: „Ich brauche gerade etwas Freiraum.“

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of brauche; etwas indicates an unspecified amount.
language_specific.usage: Mara tells her friend that she needs room for herself at present.

common.sentence: Lea zu Mara nach der Probe: „Soll ich dich ein Stück begleiten?“

language_specific.grammar: Ein Stück is an accusative distance phrase; dich is the object of begleiten. Sollen uses the replacement infinitive sollen in the perfect with a dependent infinitive.
language_specific.usage: Lea offers to walk with her choir friend for part of the journey.

common.sentence: Lea zu Chorfreund Ben: „Bitte hör auf, mir deine Hilfe aufzudrängen.“

language_specific.grammar: Aufzudrängen is the zu-infinitive following hör auf; deine Hilfe is accusative and mir is the dative recipient.
language_specific.usage: Lea asks her choir friend to stop imposing his help on her.

common.sentence: Mara zu Lea: „Meine Frage war zu persönlich; das tut mir leid.“

language_specific.grammar: Das refers to Mara's overly personal question; mir is the dative person feeling regret.
language_specific.usage: Mara acknowledges a boundary she crossed and expresses regret to her choir friend.

common.sentence: Lea zu Ben nach ihrem Streit: „Ich hätte dich ausreden lassen sollen.“

language_specific.grammar: The infinitive cluster expresses an unrealized past obligation; dich is the person Lea should have allowed to finish. Ausreden: redet aus, redete aus, ausgeredet; haben, separable. Lassen: lässt, ließ, gelassen; haben, inseparable. Sollen: soll, sollte, gesollt; haben, inseparable; with a dependent infinitive, sollen uses the replacement infinitive.

common.sentence: Ben zu Lea nach dem Streit: „Ich habe dich falsch verstanden.“

language_specific.grammar: Verstanden forms the perfect with habe; falsch modifies the participle and dich is the accusative object.
language_specific.usage: Ben acknowledges his own misunderstanding during repair with his choir friend.

common.sentence: Mara zu Ben: „Dein Witz über meine Stimme hat mich verletzt.“

language_specific.grammar: Verletzt forms the perfect with hat; mich is the accusative person emotionally hurt.
language_specific.usage: Mara tells her choir friend the effect of his joke about her voice.

common.sentence: Ben zu Mara: „Ich wollte dich mit dem Witz nicht kränken.“

language_specific.grammar: The infinitive follows wollte and takes accusative dich. With a dependent infinitive, wollen uses the replacement infinitive wollen in the perfect.
language_specific.usage: Ben explains his intention concerning the joke; nicht negates that intention.

common.sentence: Lea zu ihrer Chorfreundin Mara: „Danke, dass du mein Nein stehen lässt.“

language_specific.grammar: The verb cluster ends the dass-clause; mein Nein is accusative. Stehen: steht, stand, gestanden; auxiliary haben, inseparable. With a dependent infinitive, lassen normally uses the replacement infinitive in the perfect.
language_specific.usage: Lea thanks her choir friend for accepting her refusal without pressing her further.

common.sentence: Mara zu Lea: „Ich frage lieber erst, bevor ich dich umarme.“

language_specific.grammar: First-person singular present at the end of the bevor-clause; dich is the accusative object.
language_specific.usage: Mara signals that she will ask her choir friend before initiating a hug.

common.sentence: Lea an Ben: „Ich denke an dich und wünsche dir Kraft.“

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of wünsche; dir is the dative recipient.
language_specific.usage: Lea sends her choir friend a brief message of support.

common.sentence: Ben an Mara: „Melde dich, wenn du Gesellschaft möchtest.“

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of möchtest; Gesellschaft means another person's company here.
language_specific.usage: Ben offers his choir friend company while leaving the choice to her.

common.sentence: Mara zu Lea: „Ich bin froh, dass ich dir vertrauen kann.“

language_specific.grammar: The infinitive is governed by kann; vertrauen takes dative dir. With a dependent infinitive, können uses the replacement infinitive können in the perfect.
language_specific.usage: Mara expresses trust in her choir friend.

common.sentence: Lea zu ihrem Chorfreund Ben: „Ich verzeihe dir deine Bemerkung, brauche aber noch Zeit.“

language_specific.grammar: First-person singular present; dir is the dative person forgiven and deine Bemerkung is the accusative object.
language_specific.usage: Lea forgives her choir friend for his remark while saying she still needs time.

common.sentence: Ben zu Lea: „War mein Kommentar für dich verletzend?“

language_specific.grammar: Predicate adjective after war; für dich identifies the person potentially hurt.
language_specific.usage: Ben asks his choir friend about the effect of his comment without assuming her answer.

common.sentence: Mara zu Lea: „Ich habe meinen Text vergessen; mein Gedächtnis macht heute Pause.“
common.meaning: my memory is taking a break today

language_specific.grammar: Mein Gedächtnis is the nominative subject; Pause is the accusative object in Pause machen. Secondary noun: die Pause, plural Pausen.
language_specific.usage: Mara playfully describes her own lapse to her choir friend.

common.sentence: Mara zu Chorfreundin Lea: „Darf ich mich dir anvertrauen?“

language_specific.grammar: The infinitive follows darf; mich refers to Mara and dir is dative. With a dependent infinitive, dürfen uses the replacement infinitive in the perfect.
language_specific.usage: Mara asks her choir friend whether she can share something personal.

common.sentence: Lea zu Chorfreund Ben: „Bitte behandle meine Nachricht diskret.“

language_specific.usage: Lea asks her choir friend to handle her message without drawing unwanted attention to it.

common.sentence: Ben zu Chorfreundin Mara: „Du kannst dich auf meine Verschwiegenheit verlassen.“

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular after auf in sich auf etwas verlassen.
language_specific.usage: Ben assures his choir friend that he can keep information private.

common.sentence: Mara zu Chorfreund Ben: „Bitte hole mein Einverständnis ein, bevor du mein Foto veröffentlichst.“

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of einholen; ein closes the separable verb bracket.
language_specific.usage: Mara asks her choir friend to obtain her consent before publishing her photo.

common.sentence: Lea zu Chorfreundin Mara: „Über meine Familie möchte ich heute schweigen.“

language_specific.grammar: The infinitive follows möchte; über meine Familie identifies the topic. Mögen uses the replacement infinitive in the perfect with a dependent infinitive.
language_specific.usage: Lea tells her friend that she does not want to discuss her family today.

common.sentence: Ben zu Chorfreundin Lea: „Du musst mir keine Einzelheiten schildern.“

language_specific.grammar: Accusative plural object of schildern; mir is the dative recipient. Keine negates Einzelheiten, so the clause says that no details need to be given.
language_specific.usage: Ben relieves his friend of pressure to explain more than she wishes.

common.sentence: Mara zu Chorfreundin Lea: „Gibst du mir dein Okay, Ben von deinem Umzug zu erzählen?“

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of gibst; mir identifies the person receiving approval.
language_specific.usage: In informal speech, Mara asks her choir friend for permission to tell Ben about Lea's move.

common.sentence: Lea zu Chorfreundin Mara: „Über meinen Arzttermin sprechen wir bitte nur unter vier Augen.“

language_specific.grammar: Unter governs dative plural vier Augen in this fixed phrase.
language_specific.usage: Lea asks to discuss her appointment privately with Mara, with no one else present.

common.sentence: Ben an Chorfreundin Lea: „Du brauchst auf diese Nachricht nicht sofort zu antworten.“

language_specific.grammar: Nicht negates sofort; brauchen with zu and negation expresses absence of necessity.
language_specific.usage: Ben removes pressure for an immediate reply while leaving a later reply open.

common.sentence: Mara an Chorfreund Ben: „Soll ich einfach zuhören oder möchtest du einen Rat?“

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of möchtest; Rat means advice here, not a council.
language_specific.usage: Mara lets her choir friend choose between being heard and receiving advice.

common.sentence: Lea zu Chorfreundin Mara: „Danke, dass du mir zuhörst, ohne mich zu beurteilen.“

language_specific.grammar: The infinitive follows ohne zu; mich is the accusative person judged.
language_specific.usage: Lea appreciates her friend's listening without judgment.

common.sentence: Ben an Chorfreundin Lea: „Ich übernehme morgen gern den Fahrdienst zu deiner Untersuchung.“

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of übernehme; den Fahrdienst übernehmen means to take responsibility for driving someone.
language_specific.usage: Ben offers his choir friend a ride to her examination.

common.sentence: Mara zu Chorfreund Ben: „Danke für dein offenes Ohr nach der Probe.“

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular after für; offenes has a mixed ending after dein.
language_specific.usage: The expression thanks Ben for listening sympathetically to his choir friend.

common.sentence: Ben zu Chorfreundin Lea: „Soll ich für dich einkaufen?“ Lea: „Das ist lieb von dir, aber ich schaffe es allein.“

language_specific.grammar: Lieb is predicative after ist; von dir identifies Ben as the person offering help.
language_specific.usage: Lea warmly acknowledges her choir friend's offer while declining help with the shopping.

common.sentence: Ben zu Chorfreundin Mara: „Ich verspreche dir, dass ich mir morgen für dich Zeit nehme.“

language_specific.grammar: Zeit is the accusative object of nehme, which is final in the dass-clause; mir is dative and refers to Ben.
language_specific.usage: Ben promises to make time for his choir friend the next day.

common.sentence: Mara zu Chorfreundin Lea: „Ich bin gerade überfordert und brauche eine Pause.“

language_specific.grammar: Predicate adjective after bin; it describes Mara's present state.
language_specific.usage: Mara tells her friend that her current demands exceed what she can manage.

common.sentence: Lea an Chorfreundin Mara: „Soll ich dir morgen das Abendessen vorbeibringen?“

language_specific.grammar: The infinitive follows soll; dir is dative and das Abendessen accusative. Sollen uses the replacement infinitive in the perfect with a dependent infinitive.
language_specific.usage: Lea offers her choir friend a specific meal.

common.sentence: Ben zu Chorfreundin Lea: „Ich hätte vor meinem Besuch fragen müssen.“

language_specific.grammar: With hätte, the infinitive cluster expresses an unrealized past obligation. Müssen: muss, musste, gemusst; haben, inseparable; with a dependent infinitive its perfect uses the replacement infinitive müssen.
language_specific.usage: Ben acknowledges that he should have asked his choir friend before visiting.

common.sentence: Lea zu Chorfreund Ben: „Dein unangekündigter Besuch hat mich überrumpelt.“

language_specific.grammar: The participle forms the perfect with hat; mich is the accusative person caught off guard.
language_specific.usage: Lea explains the effect of her friend's unannounced visit.

common.sentence: Mara zu Chorfreundin Lea: „Ich war gestern ungerecht zu dir.“

language_specific.grammar: Predicate adjective after war; zu dir identifies the person treated unfairly.
language_specific.usage: Mara takes responsibility for how she treated her choir friend.

common.sentence: Ben zu Chorfreundin Mara: „Ich bereue, dass ich deinen Fehler vor allen weitererzählt habe.“

language_specific.grammar: First-person singular present; the dass-clause states what Ben regrets.
language_specific.usage: Ben expresses regret for telling the group about his choir friend's mistake.

common.sentence: Mara zu Chorfreund Ben: „Ich möchte verstehen, was dich an meiner Bemerkung geärgert hat.“

language_specific.grammar: The participle forms the perfect with hat; dich is the accusative person annoyed, and was is the subject.
language_specific.usage: Mara asks her choir friend to explain what bothered him about her remark.

common.sentence: Lea zu Chorfreundin Mara: „Ich habe deine Nachricht als Vorwurf aufgefasst.“

language_specific.grammar: The participle forms the perfect with habe; deine Nachricht is accusative and als Vorwurf gives Lea's interpretation.
language_specific.usage: Lea describes her own reading of her friend's message.

common.sentence: Mara zu Chorfreundin Lea: „Dich mit meiner Nachricht zu verletzen, war nicht meine Absicht.“

language_specific.grammar: Meine Absicht is a nominative predicate phrase after war; nicht negates it.
language_specific.usage: Mara clarifies that she did not intend to hurt her choir friend with the message.

common.sentence: Ben zu Chorfreundin Lea: „Ich sehe ein, dass meine Bemerkung unfair war.“

language_specific.grammar: First-person singular present with separable ein; the dass-clause states what Ben recognizes.
language_specific.usage: Ben acknowledges the unfairness of his own remark to his choir friend.

common.sentence: Lea zu Chorfreund Ben: „Lass uns später weiterreden; ich bin noch wütend.“

language_specific.grammar: The infinitive follows lass; uns includes Lea and Ben. Lassen normally uses the replacement infinitive in the perfect with a dependent infinitive.
language_specific.usage: Lea proposes postponing the discussion because she is still angry.

common.sentence: Ben zu Chorfreundin Mara: „Ich will deine Gefühle nicht herunterspielen.“

language_specific.grammar: The infinitive follows will; deine Gefühle is accusative and nicht negates Ben's intention. Wollen uses the replacement infinitive in the perfect with a dependent infinitive.
language_specific.usage: Ben says he does not want to dismiss the importance of his friend's feelings.

common.sentence: Mara zu Chorfreundin Lea: „Dein Schweigen nach meinem Anruf hat mich verunsichert.“

language_specific.grammar: The participle forms the perfect with hat; mich is the accusative person affected.
language_specific.usage: Mara describes how her friend's silence after the call affected her.

common.sentence: Lea zu Chorfreundin Mara: „Ich war erschöpft; mein Schweigen galt nicht dir.“

language_specific.grammar: Galt is preterite; dir is the dative person at whom the silence was not directed.
language_specific.usage: Lea explains that her silence reflected exhaustion rather than a message to Mara.

common.sentence: Ben zu Chorfreundin Lea: „Ich möchte meinen Fehler wiedergutmachen.“

language_specific.grammar: The infinitive follows möchte; meinen Fehler is accusative. Mögen uses the replacement infinitive in the perfect with a dependent infinitive.
language_specific.usage: Ben expresses a wish to make amends to his choir friend for his mistake.

common.sentence: Lea zu Chorfreund Ben: „Ein bisschen Geduld würde mir jetzt helfen.“

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular head of the subject phrase ein bisschen Geduld; mir is dative after helfen.
language_specific.usage: Lea tells her choir friend what would help her now.

common.sentence: Ben lädt Chorfreundin Mara zum Konzert ein; sie antwortet: „Ich möchte darüber schlafen.“

language_specific.grammar: The infinitive follows möchte; darüber refers to Ben's invitation. Mögen uses the replacement infinitive in the perfect with a dependent infinitive.
language_specific.usage: Mara wants time to consider the invitation before deciding.

common.sentence: Ben zu Chorfreundin Mara: „Ich werde dich wegen meiner Konzerteinladung nicht drängen.“

language_specific.grammar: The infinitive follows werde; dich is the accusative person. Nicht negates drängen, so Ben commits to withholding pressure.
language_specific.usage: Ben assures his choir friend that he will not rush her response to his invitation.

common.sentence: Lea zu Chorfreundin Mara: „Deine ehrliche Rückmeldung bedeutet mir viel.“

language_specific.grammar: Bedeutet is third-person singular; mir is dative and viel expresses the degree of importance.
language_specific.usage: Lea tells her choir friend that she values the honest feedback.

common.sentence: Ben zu Chorfreundin Lea: „Ich nannte deinen Gesang Froschgequake. War das als Witz erkennbar?“

language_specific.grammar: The phrase is predicative after war; als Witz identifies how the remark might be recognized.
language_specific.usage: Ben checks whether his comparison of his choir friend's singing to frogs was recognizable as humor.

common.sentence: Lea zu Chorfreund Ben: „Deinen Witz über meine Stimme finde ich daneben.“

language_specific.grammar: Daneben is the object complement of finde; deinen Witz is accusative.
language_specific.usage: In informal speech, Lea tells her choir friend that his joke about her voice was inappropriate.

common.sentence: Ben zu Chorfreundin Lea: „Ich werde solche Witze über deine Stimme künftig sein lassen.“

language_specific.grammar: Sein lassen follows werde; solche Witze is accusative. Sein: ist, war, gewesen; auxiliary sein, inseparable. Lassen: lässt, ließ, gelassen; auxiliary haben, inseparable. With a dependent infinitive, lassen normally uses the replacement infinitive in the perfect: hat sein lassen.
language_specific.usage: Ben tells his choir friend that he will stop making jokes about her voice.

common.sentence: Mara zu Chorfreundin Lea: „Ich habe meinen Einsatz verpasst; mein Einsatz hat mich wohl auch verpasst.“

language_specific.grammar: Hat verpasst is the perfect; mich is accusative and wohl marks the playful inference. Secondary auxiliary haben: hat, hatte, gehabt; auxiliary haben, inseparable.
language_specific.usage: Mara jokes about her own missed entry by giving the entry an impossible ability to miss her.

common.sentence: Lea zu Chorfreund Ben: „War mein Kommentar eben zu schroff?“

language_specific.grammar: Predicate adjective after war; zu marks a potentially excessive degree.
language_specific.usage: Lea checks whether her recent comment sounded too abrupt to her choir friend.

common.sentence: Ben zu Chorfreundin Lea: „Ja, aber ich weiß deine Nachfrage zu schätzen.“

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of zu schätzen wissen; deine identifies Lea's question.
language_specific.usage: Ben appreciates his choir friend's follow-up question.

common.sentence: Mara zu Chorfreundin Lea: „Dein Zuspruch vor der Probe hat mir geholfen.“

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject; vor der Probe identifies when Lea gave encouragement.
language_specific.usage: Mara tells her choir friend that her encouragement helped.

common.sentence: Lea an Chorfreund Ben: „Deine Nachricht hat mich aufgemuntert.“

language_specific.grammar: The participle forms the perfect with hat; mich is the accusative person cheered up.
language_specific.usage: Lea tells her choir friend that his message lifted her spirits.

common.sentence: Ben zu Chorfreundin Mara: „Deine Absage nehme ich dir nicht krumm.“
common.meaning: separable verb prefix in resent someone for something

language_specific.grammar: Krumm completes the separable verb krummnehmen; deine Absage is accusative and dir is dative.
language_specific.usage: Ben assures Mara that he does not resent her refusal. The expression is informal.

common.sentence: Mara zu Chorfreund Ben: „Ich möchte selbst bestimmen, wer mich zu Hause besucht.“

language_specific.grammar: The infinitive follows möchte; the wer-clause states what Mara wants to decide.
language_specific.usage: Mara asserts her choice over who visits her home.

common.sentence: Lea zu Chorfreundin Mara: „Deine Offenheit macht es mir leichter, ehrlich zu sein.“

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject; deine identifies Mara's openness.
language_specific.usage: Lea explains how her friend's openness helps her speak honestly.

common.sentence: Ben an Chorfreundin Lea: „Nach deiner Operation erledige ich gern deine Einkäufe.“

language_specific.grammar: Accusative plural object of erledige; deine identifies the shopping Ben offers to do for Lea.
language_specific.usage: Ben offers practical help to his choir friend after her operation.

common.sentence: Mara zu Chorfreundin Lea: „Bitte verrate Ben meinen neuen Wohnort noch nicht.“

language_specific.grammar: Second-person singular imperative; Ben is the dative recipient and meinen neuen Wohnort the accusative information.
language_specific.usage: Mara asks Lea not to reveal her new place of residence to Ben yet.

common.sentence: Lea zu Chorfreundin Mara: „Ich respektiere deinen Wunsch nach Ungestörtheit.“

language_specific.grammar: Dative singular after nach; the phrase specifies the wish Lea respects.
language_specific.usage: Lea acknowledges Mara's wish to be left undisturbed.

common.sentence: Ben zu Chorfreundin Lea: „Deine Zusage gibt mir Rückhalt bei der Chorversammlung.“

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of gibt; mir is the dative recipient. Jemandem Rückhalt geben means to give someone backing.
language_specific.usage: Ben tells Lea that her commitment gives him support at the choir meeting.

common.sentence: Mara an Chorfreund Ben: „Lass uns nach deiner Reise in Verbindung bleiben.“

language_specific.usage: The delay occurs before Lea starts her answer; it does not by itself reveal her motive.

common.sentence: Lea fragt nach Samstag; Ben setzt das Verzögerungssignal „Äh“ vor sein „Nein“.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of setzt; vor sein „Nein“ marks the position before the refusal.
language_specific.usage: The hesitation sound äh precedes Ben's negative answer.

common.sentence: Lea spricht noch; Ben sagt „mhm“ als Rückmeldesignal, ohne ihren Satz zu übernehmen.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular after als, describing the function of mhm.
language_specific.usage: Ben signals attention while Lea continues; mhm alone does not establish agreement.

common.sentence: Mara beendet ihren Satz; Ben nutzt die mögliche Übergabestelle für seinen Einwand.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of nutzt; für introduces Ben's intended contribution.
language_specific.usage: The end of Mara's sentence provides a possible point for another speaker to begin.

common.sentence: Nach Leas Frage erfolgt ein Sprecherwechsel: Ben antwortet auf ihre Kritik.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of erfolgt; the following clause identifies Ben taking the next turn.
language_specific.usage: The term identifies the change from Lea speaking to Ben speaking.

common.sentence: Lea fragt nach Hilfe; Bens Schweigen lässt die Antworterwartung unerfüllt.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of lässt.
language_specific.usage: Lea's request makes a response relevant; Ben's silence leaves that expectation unmet.

common.sentence: Ben bietet Lea Tee an; ihre Angebotsannahme lautet „Gern“.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of lautet.
language_specific.usage: Lea's gern accepts Ben's offer of tea.

common.sentence: Lea bittet Ben um Hilfe für morgen; seine Antwort „Ich arbeite morgen den ganzen Tag“ ist eine implizite Ablehnung.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular predicate phrase after ist; implizite has a mixed ending after eine.
language_specific.usage: Ben's statement can be understood as declining Lea's request without explicitly saying no.

common.sentence: Ben: „Es zieht am Fenster.“ Lea: „Ich mache es zu.“

language_specific.grammar: Impersonal es is the subject of zieht; am Fenster locates the draft.
language_specific.usage: Lea treats Ben's observation as a reason to close the window; the observation can function as an indirect request.

common.sentence: Lea fragt in einer Präsequenz nach Bens Zeit; nach seinem Ja lädt sie ihn zur Chorprobe ein.

language_specific.grammar: Dative singular after in, locating the question within the preliminary sequence.
language_specific.usage: Lea checks Ben's availability before making the invitation.

common.sentence: Ben nennt Leas Vorschlag „mutig“ und erklärt: „Ich halte ihn für zu teuer.“

language_specific.grammar: Uninflected object complement of nennt, referring to Leas Vorschlag.
language_specific.usage: The follow-up makes Ben's criticism explicit; mutig alone could also be praise.

common.sentence: Lea: „Dein Vorschlag ist interessant; bezahlen können wir ihn leider nicht.“

language_specific.grammar: Predicate adjective after ist.
language_specific.usage: Lea acknowledges the proposal positively before explaining why the group cannot afford it.

common.sentence: Lea schlägt Montag vor; Ben entgegnet: „Ich habe Bauchweh bei diesem Termin.“

language_specific.grammar: Accusative object in Bauchweh bei etwas haben; bei takes the dative.
language_specific.usage: Register: informal. Ben informally expresses reservations about Lea's proposed date without yet explaining them.

common.sentence: Lea lehnt die Chorfreizeit ab; Ben fragt: „Was gibt den Ausschlag?“

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object in den Ausschlag geben; was is the subject.
language_specific.usage: Ben asks which consideration is decisive for Lea's refusal.

common.sentence: Mara beendet ihren Beitrag und wählt niemanden; Ben beginnt durch Selbstwahl.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular after durch.
language_specific.usage: At a possible transition point, Ben starts speaking without having been selected by Mara.

common.sentence: Mara fragt „Lea, was meinst du?“; diese Fremdwahl bestimmt Lea als nächste Sprecherin.
common.meaning: selection of the next speaker by the current speaker

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of bestimmt.
language_specific.usage: Mara's question addresses Lea and selects her to speak next.

common.sentence: Ben lehnt den Chorauftritt ab; Leas Redezug beginnt mit einer Nachfrage.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of beginnt.
language_specific.usage: A Redezug is a contribution by one speaker; Lea's begins after Ben's refusal.

common.sentence: Lea lädt Ben ein; seine Rückfrage nach dem Tag klärt sie vor seiner Zusage in einer Einschubsequenz.

language_specific.grammar: Dative singular after in; the phrase describes the sequence in which the day is clarified.
language_specific.usage: The clarification comes between Lea's invitation and Ben's acceptance.

common.sentence: Ben kritisiert die kurze Probe; Lea bittet um Konkretisierung.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular after um in um etwas bitten.
language_specific.usage: Lea asks Ben to make his criticism more concrete.

common.sentence: Lea: „Ich möchte leiser proben.“ Ben: „Geht es dir um die Nachbarn?“

language_specific.grammar: Geht begins the question; dir is dative, and um governs accusative die Nachbarn.
language_specific.usage: Ben proposes a possible concern for Lea to confirm or reject.

common.sentence: Lea und Ben bestehen beide darauf, ihren Beitrag zu beenden; ihr Kampf um das Rederecht endet, als Ben nachgibt.
common.meaning: competition for the right to speak

language_specific.grammar: Kampf is the nominative singular subject of endet; um governs accusative das Rederecht. Rederecht is neuter, plural Rederechte.
language_specific.usage: Lea and Ben both insist on finishing their contributions; Ben eventually yields the floor.

common.sentence: Mara: „Ben, du bist als Nächster dran.“ Lea wartet mit ihrem Einwand.

language_specific.grammar: Nächster is a nominalized adjective with a strong nominative masculine singular ending, referring to Ben.
language_specific.usage: Mara assigns Ben the next turn; Lea waits before making her objection.

common.sentence: Lea spricht noch; Ben hebt die Hand als Redeanmeldung.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular after als, describing the function of Ben's gesture.
language_specific.usage: Ben signals that he wants a later turn while Lea is still speaking.

common.sentence: Ben: „Ich bin noch nicht überzeugt.“ Lea: „Was müsste sich ändern?“

language_specific.grammar: Müsste is Konjunktiv II and governs ändern; sich is reflexive. With a dependent infinitive, the perfect uses the replacement infinitive müssen. Sich ändern: ändert sich, änderte sich, hat sich geändert; inseparable.
language_specific.usage: Lea asks Ben what change could address his reservation without assuming that one will.

common.sentence: Ben nimmt Leas Einladung an; ihr „Das freut mich“ bildet eine Postsequenz.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of bildet.
language_specific.usage: Lea's expression of pleasure follows Ben's acceptance and expands the completed invitation exchange.

common.sentence: Leas Frage nach dem Probentermin und Bens Antwort „Montag“ bilden eine Paarsequenz.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of bilden.
language_specific.usage: Lea's question makes an answer relevant; Ben supplies the requested day.

common.sentence: Ben nennt Leas Einwand „pingelig“; sie fragt: „Wie kommst du darauf?“

language_specific.grammar: Kommst agrees with du; darauf refers to Ben's assessment.
language_specific.usage: Lea asks Ben to explain the basis for calling her objection picky; the question can challenge his assessment.

common.sentence: Leas Selbstinitiierung: „Wir proben am … welcher Tag war das noch mal?“

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular in an elliptical label for Lea's utterance.
language_specific.usage: Lea signals trouble recalling the day in her own utterance; no completed repair is shown.

common.sentence: Die Chorleiterin entzieht Ben das Wort und bittet Lea um ihre Stellungnahme.

language_specific.grammar: Entzieht is third-person singular; Ben is dative and das Wort is accusative in jemandem das Wort entziehen.
language_specific.usage: The choir leader ends Ben's speaking turn and invites Lea to state her view.

common.sentence: Ben lehnt das Chorfest ab; Lea fragt: „Was genau missfällt dir daran?“

language_specific.grammar: Was is the subject; dir is dative, and daran refers to the choir event.
language_specific.usage: Lea asks Ben to identify what he dislikes about the event.

common.sentence: Lea: „Das Lied passt nicht.“ Ben: „Was spricht dagegen?“

language_specific.grammar: Was is the subject of spricht; dagegen refers to choosing the song.
language_specific.usage: Ben asks Lea for the reasons behind her negative assessment without supplying them himself.

common.sentence: Ben: „Wir sollten warten.“ Lea: „Bis die anderen zurück sind?“

language_specific.grammar: Bis introduces a time clause with finite sind at the end; die anderen is the weak plural subject.
language_specific.usage: Lea proposes an endpoint for Ben's suggested wait and asks him to confirm it.

common.sentence: Lea: „Das war unfreundlich.“ Ben: „Meinst du meine Worte oder meinen Ton?“

language_specific.grammar: Both alternatives are accusative objects of meinst. Ton is masculine, plural Töne; Worte refers to connected words or remarks.
language_specific.usage: Ben asks whether Lea's criticism concerns what he said or how he said it.

common.sentence: Lea stockt: „Wir proben im … wie heißt der Raum?“ Bens Fremdreparatur: „Saal B.“

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular in an elliptical label for Ben's contribution.
language_specific.usage: Lea signals trouble recalling the room's name; Ben supplies it.

common.sentence: Lea trägt allein die Noten; Ben fragt: „Kann ich dir etwas abnehmen?“

language_specific.grammar: Abnehmen is an infinitive governed by kann; etwas is accusative and dir is dative. With a dependent infinitive, können uses the replacement infinitive können in the perfect.
language_specific.usage: Ben offers to carry some of the music Lea is carrying.

common.sentence: Ben sitzt vor der Sparkasse auf einer Sitzbank: „Meine Bank hat Filialen und Holzlatten“, sagt er zu Freundin Lea.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of hat.
language_specific.usage: Ben jokes with his friend Lea by combining features of a financial institution and a bench.

common.sentence: Ben: „Am Schloss fehlt der Schlüssel, am anderen der Turm.“ Lea lacht über die Zweideutigkeit.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular after über in über etwas lachen.
language_specific.usage: Ben plays on Schloss as both a lock and a castle.

common.sentence: Ben: „Der Chor hat viele Stimmen, aber bei der Abstimmung nur eine.“ Lea lacht über sein Wortspiel.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular after über in über etwas lachen.
language_specific.usage: Ben plays on Stimmen as singing voices and votes.

common.sentence: Lea nennt Bens Wortspiel einen Kalauer und verdreht lachend die Augen.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular predicate noun after nennt.
language_specific.usage: Lea treats Ben's wordplay as a groan-worthy joke; her laughter makes the criticism playful.

common.sentence: Ben erzählt: „Treffen sich zwei Töne. Sagt der eine: Du bist aber hochgestimmt.“

language_specific.grammar: Predicate adjective after bist.
language_specific.usage: The adjective normally describes a cheerful mood; applied to a musical note, it also evokes a high pitch.

common.sentence: Bei jeder Chorprobe fällt Bens Stift; Leas Running Gag lautet: „Abflug!“

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of lautet.
language_specific.usage: Lea repeatedly calls the pen's fall a takeoff, making the recurring mishap a shared joke.

common.sentence: Nach dem Rohrbruch witzelt Lea: „Endlich ein Schwimmbad.“ Ben erkennt ihren Galgenhumor.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of erkennt.
language_specific.usage: Lea jokes about the flooding in an unpleasant situation.

common.sentence: Ben nennt seinen gescheiterten Auftritt „eine Sternstunde“; Lea erkennt den Selbstspott.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of erkennt.
language_specific.usage: Ben mocks his own failed performance by calling it an outstanding moment.

common.sentence: Lea rutscht auf der Bühne aus; Ben erklärt den Sturz zum Slapstick.

language_specific.grammar: Dative singular after zum, the contraction of zu dem, in etwas zu etwas erklären.
language_specific.usage: Ben describes the fall as physical comedy; the sentence does not say Lea intended it.

common.sentence: „Nicht ganz optimal“, sagt Mara: Der Saal ist für alle hundert Gäste gesperrt.

language_specific.grammar: Nicht ganz modifies the elliptical adjective optimal.
language_specific.usage: Mara's mild assessment understates the consequence of the hall being closed to every guest.

common.sentence: „Das hat Potenzial“, sagt Ben lachend über seinen ungenießbar salzigen Eintopf.

language_specific.grammar: Hat is third-person singular; Potenzial is its accusative object. The contextual collocation is Potenzial haben.
language_specific.usage: Ben humorously offers a hopeful assessment of his own inedible dish.

common.sentence: Der Chor singt den Schluss dreimal falsch; Lea nennt das „ausbaufähig“.

language_specific.grammar: Uninflected object complement after nennt.
language_specific.usage: Lea humorously softens criticism of the repeated mistakes by stressing the possibility of improvement.

common.sentence: Ben bezeichnet den stundenlangen Streit um einen Stuhl als „kleine Meinungsverschiedenheit“.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular predicate phrase after als in etwas als etwas bezeichnen; kleine is part of the mild characterization.
language_specific.usage: Together with kleine, the noun presents the lengthy dispute mildly.

common.sentence: Nach dem Chorstreit sagt Lea zu Ben: „Lass uns einen Neuanfang wagen.“

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object in einen Neuanfang wagen.
language_specific.usage: Lea invites Ben to make a fresh start together after their dispute.

common.sentence: Lea: „Du hast mich vor allen unterbrochen.“ Ben: „Ich bitte dich um Vergebung.“

language_specific.grammar: Um governs accusative Vergebung; dich is the person addressed by bitten.
language_specific.usage: Ben explicitly asks Lea to forgive him; the wording is solemn.

common.sentence: Ben: „Dein Vorschlag ist Unsinn.“ Lea: „Kannst du das weniger abwertend sagen?“

language_specific.grammar: Weniger modifies abwertend, which describes how Ben might phrase his criticism.
language_specific.usage: Lea challenges the disparaging wording while leaving room for Ben to restate his objection.

common.sentence: Ben: „Niemand mag den Saal.“ Lea: „Das ist eine Unterstellung; ich mag ihn.“

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular predicate noun after ist.
language_specific.usage: Lea challenges Ben's attribution of the same opinion to everyone and gives a counterexample.

common.sentence: Lea: „Wir wechseln den Saal.“ Bens Verständnisfrage: „Ins Rathaus?“

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular head of an elliptical label introducing Ben's question.
language_specific.usage: Ben checks whether Lea means a move to the town hall; he does not assume she does.

common.sentence: Lea: „Die Miete ist zu hoch.“ Ben: „Das Argument hat Gewicht, auch wenn ich bleiben möchte.“

language_specific.grammar: Hat is third-person singular; Gewicht is its accusative object.
language_specific.usage: Ben acknowledges the force of Lea's argument while expressing a different preference.

common.sentence: Lea nennt den Saal zu teuer; Bens „Diskussion beendet!“ bezeichnet sie als Gesprächskiller.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular predicate noun after als in etwas als etwas bezeichnen.
language_specific.usage: Lea characterizes Ben's declaration as shutting down discussion of the hall's cost.

common.sentence: Lea: „Ich bin verletzt.“ Ben: „Das wollte ich nicht; ich höre dir zu.“

language_specific.grammar: Wollte is first-person singular preterite; das refers to Lea's being hurt.
language_specific.usage: Ben denies intending the hurt and offers to listen; he does not deny Lea's experience.

common.sentence: Lea: „Ich möchte allein sein.“ Ben: „Ich gebe dir Raum.“

language_specific.grammar: Gebe is first-person singular; dir is dative and Raum is accusative.
language_specific.usage: Ben accepts Lea's request for solitude and signals that he will leave her space.

common.sentence: Lea: „Dein Witz hat mich verletzt.“ Ben: „Ich habe mich im Ton vergriffen.“

language_specific.grammar: Im contracts in dem and takes dative Ton; mich is the reflexive pronoun, and vergriffen forms the perfect with habe.
language_specific.usage: Ben acknowledges that the way he spoke to Lea was inappropriate.

common.sentence: Ben: „Die Probe dauert mir zu lange.“ Lea: „Können wir uns auf zwei Stunden einigen?“

language_specific.grammar: Uns is reflexive; auf governs accusative zwei Stunden. Einigen follows können, which uses the replacement infinitive in the perfect with a dependent infinitive.
language_specific.usage: Lea proposes a specific duration for Ben and herself to agree on.

common.sentence: Lea: „Dein Witz über mich tat weh.“ Ben: „Ich verspreche Besserung.“

language_specific.grammar: Verspreche is first-person singular; Besserung is the accusative object.
language_specific.usage: Ben promises to improve his behavior after Lea says the joke hurt her.

common.sentence: Ben: „Lea singt schief, Mara plant schlecht, der Chor klingt furchtbar.“ Lea: „Was für ein Rundumschlag!“

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular in an elliptical exclamation with was für ein.
language_specific.usage: Lea characterizes Ben's criticism of two individuals and the choir as a sweeping attack.

common.sentence: Lea: „Draußen ist es billiger.“ Ben: „Drinnen bleibt es trocken; lass uns beides gegeneinander abwägen.“

language_specific.grammar: The infinitive follows lass; beides refers to lower cost outdoors and dry conditions indoors. Lassen uses a replacement infinitive in the perfect with a dependent infinitive.
language_specific.usage: Ben proposes weighing the two stated advantages against each other.

common.sentence: Ben: „Du übertreibst.“ Lea: „Bitte lass mich erst erklären, was passiert ist.“

language_specific.grammar: Lass is the informal singular imperative; mich is accusative and erklären is the dependent infinitive. Erklären: erklärt, erklärte, erklärt; auxiliary haben; inseparable. Lassen uses the replacement infinitive lassen in the perfect with a dependent infinitive.
language_specific.usage: Lea asks Ben to hear her account before judging it.

common.sentence: Lea: „Ich bin enttäuscht.“ Ben: „Magst du erzählen, was dich enttäuscht hat?“

language_specific.grammar: Magst is second-person singular and governs erzählen. Erzählen: erzählt, erzählte, erzählt; auxiliary haben; inseparable. Mögen uses the replacement infinitive mögen in the perfect with a dependent infinitive.
language_specific.usage: Ben invites Lea to explain her disappointment while leaving her free to decline.

common.sentence: Ben: „Ich möchte nicht darüber reden.“ Lea: „Das ist für mich in Ordnung.“

language_specific.grammar: In governs dative singular Ordnung in the predicate phrase in Ordnung sein.
language_specific.usage: Lea accepts Ben's wish not to discuss the matter.

common.sentence: Bei der Chorbesprechung reden Lea und Ben zugleich; Mara bittet um Redepausen.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative plural after um in um etwas bitten.
language_specific.usage: Mara requests pauses so that the overlapping speakers can give each other room.

common.sentence: Lea: „Ben, ich bin noch mitten im Satz.“ Ben: „Entschuldige, sprich weiter.“
common.meaning: in the middle of a sentence

language_specific.grammar: Im contracts in dem; Satz is dative singular after in.
language_specific.usage: Lea says she is still in the middle of her sentence; Ben apologizes and invites her to continue.

common.sentence: Ben: „Ich habe noch einen Gedanken.“ Lea: „Ich bin gleich fertig.“

language_specific.grammar: Gleich modifies the predicate adjective fertig after bin.
language_specific.usage: Lea signals that her turn will end soon, responding to Ben's wish to contribute.

common.sentence: Lea bricht ihren Satz ab; Ben wartet nach ihrer Selbstunterbrechung auf die Fortsetzung.

language_specific.grammar: Dative singular after nach; ihrer refers to Lea.
language_specific.usage: Lea stops her own unfinished sentence, and Ben waits for her to continue.

common.sentence: Ben: „Der Saal ist teuer.“ Lea: „Verglichen mit unserem Budget, meinst du?“

language_specific.grammar: Verglichen is a participle used in an elliptical comparison; mit governs dative unserem Budget.
language_specific.usage: Lea proposes the choir's budget as Ben's standard of comparison and asks him to confirm.

common.sentence: Lea fragt Ben: „Findest du den Chor auch zu laut?“ Ben kritisiert die Suggestivfrage.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of kritisiert.
language_specific.usage: Lea's auch suggests that someone already finds the choir too loud, prompting Ben toward agreement.

common.sentence: Lea: „Samstag kann ich nicht.“ Ben: „Schade, dann suchen wir weiter.“

language_specific.usage: Ben expresses disappointment about Saturday while accepting Lea's answer and proposing to keep looking.

common.sentence: Ben: „Dein Vorschlag passt mir nicht.“ Lea: „Gut, dass du Klartext redest.“

language_specific.grammar: Redest is second-person singular at the end of the dass-clause; Klartext is the accusative object.
language_specific.usage: Lea welcomes Ben's direct statement even though he disagrees with her proposal.

common.sentence: Lea liest in einem Schweizer Roman: „Merci vielmal!“ und versteht den ausdrücklichen Dank.

language_specific.usage: The quoted expression conveys warm thanks.
language_specific.recognition: Recognition: quoted regional Swiss expression of thanks, attested in Swiss German use; a neutral de-DE equivalent is „Vielen Dank“. This label does not claim exclusive dialect use.

common.sentence: Ben liest im Schweizer Roman „Grüezi miteinander“ und erkennt eine Begrüßung an mehrere Personen.

language_specific.usage: The greeting addresses several people together.
language_specific.recognition: Recognition: quoted regional Swiss greeting to a group; a neutral de-DE equivalent is „Guten Tag zusammen“. Its use in Swiss German does not establish exclusive dialect use.

common.sentence: Mara liest im österreichischen Plan die „Flächenwidmung“ für das Ufergrundstück.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of liest; für identifies the property concerned.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: Flächenwidmung designates the intended use of land; Flächennutzung is a useful German description, although planning systems differ.

common.sentence: Der „Flächenwidmungsplan“ aus Graz zeigt Mara die vorgesehenen Nutzungen.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of zeigt; Mara is the dative recipient.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: Flächenwidmungsplan is an Austrian planning term. Flächennutzungsplan is a related German term; the legal instruments differ.

common.sentence: Im österreichischen Projektbericht prüft die „Umweltanwaltschaft“ mögliche Folgen für die Natur.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of prüft.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: Umweltanwaltschaft names an institutional advocate for environmental interests. An equivalent German description depends on the body's role.

common.sentence: Die Einladung aus Tirol nennt eine „Bauverhandlung“ zum geplanten Steg.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of nennt; zum geplanten Steg identifies the project.
language_specific.recognition: Austria recognition: Bauverhandlung refers to a hearing in building proceedings. Verhandlung im Bauverfahren is a descriptive de-DE equivalent.

common.sentence: Mara vergleicht den Schweizer „Richtplan“ mit dem deutschen Planungsdokument.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of vergleicht; mit introduces the document used for comparison.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Richtplan is a Swiss Standard German spatial-planning term. Raumplanerischer Rahmenplan describes it in de-DE; instruments differ.

common.sentence: Der Schweizer „Nutzungsplan“ legt die zulässige Nutzung des Gebiets fest.

language_specific.grammar: Nominative singular subject of legt fest.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Nutzungsplan is a Swiss Standard German planning term. A German Bebauungsplan is a related instrument, with different rules.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Plan liegt die Wiese außerhalb der „Bauzone“.

language_specific.grammar: Genitive singular after außerhalb.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Bauzone is a Swiss Standard German planning designation. Baugebiet is a useful de-DE comparison; the legal categories differ.

common.sentence: Der Schweizer Bericht nennt die Umwandlung von Bauland in Nichtbauland „Auszonung“.
common.meaning: removal of land from a building zone

language_specific.grammar: Accusative naming complement after nennt, referring to the stated conversion.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Auszonung is a Swiss Standard German planning term. Herausnahme aus der Bauzone describes it in de-DE.

common.sentence: Die Schweizer Vorlage bezeichnet die Zuweisung zur Bauzone als „Einzonung“.
common.meaning: inclusion of land in a building zone

language_specific.grammar: Accusative complement after als in bezeichnet; it names the stated assignment.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Einzonung is a Swiss Standard German planning term. Zuweisung zur Bauzone is a suitable de-DE description.

common.sentence: Mara findet im Schweizer Plan einen „Gewässerraum“ entlang des Bachs.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of findet; entlang des Bachs locates the area.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Gewässerraum is a Swiss Standard German planning and water-protection term. Raum für das Gewässer is a de-DE description; regulations differ.

common.sentence: Der Schweizer Bericht zählt den fruchtbaren Acker zur „Fruchtfolgefläche“.

language_specific.grammar: Dative singular after zur, contracted from zu der, in etwas zu etwas zählen.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Fruchtfolgefläche is a Swiss Standard German planning category for designated high-quality agricultural land. Ackerfläche is a broader de-DE description.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Bericht bezeichnet „Mitwirkung“ die Beteiligung der Bevölkerung an der Planung.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet; plural is uncommon in this sense.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Mitwirkung is used in Swiss Standard German planning for public participation. Beteiligung der Öffentlichkeit is a de-DE description; procedures differ.

common.sentence: Die Gemeinde in Zürich legt den „Gestaltungsplan“ für das Areal vor.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of legt vor; für das Areal identifies its scope.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Gestaltungsplan is a Swiss Standard German planning instrument. Bebauungsplan is a related German term; the instruments are not identical.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Bericht bezeichnet „Siedlungsgebiet“ den Bereich für die Siedlungsentwicklung.

language_specific.grammar: The quoted nominative singular is the subject of bezeichnet.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Siedlungsgebiet is used in Swiss Standard German spatial planning. Siedlungsbereich is a possible de-DE description; planning categories differ.

common.sentence: Der Schweizer Projektbrief nennt die vorgesehene Fläche ein „Baufeld“.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular naming complement after nennt.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Baufeld is used in Swiss Standard German planning and also in Germany; Baufeld is suitable for de-DE production.

common.sentence: Der Schweizer Bericht nennt den Bachabschnitt ein „Fliessgewässer“.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular naming complement after nennt.
language_specific.recognition: Switzerland recognition: Fliessgewässer is the Swiss Standard German spelling; write Fließgewässer in de-DE.

common.sentence: Im Schweizer Plan bezeichnet „Veloabstellplatz“ einen Stellplatz für Fahrräder.

common.sentence: Ben fragt nach dem Textanfang, nicht nach dem Schluss.

language_specific.grammar: Dative singular after nach in fragen nach.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ˈtɛkstˌʔanfaŋ]: Text has short open-mid [ɛ]; Anfang begins with short [a] and may have a glottal onset. The target can be prominent against Schluss.

common.sentence: Mara nennt die Baukosten ohne Unterhalt; dessen Kosten folgen später.

language_specific.grammar: Ohne governs accusative singular Unterhalt; dessen refers back to Unterhalt.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ˈoːnə ˈʊntɐhalt]: ohne has long close-mid [oː]; Unterhalt begins with stressed short lax [ʊ]. Prominence on Unterhalt can highlight the exclusion.

common.sentence: Lea spricht langsamer als Ben, damit der Text verständlich bleibt.

language_specific.grammar: The comparative modifies spricht; als Ben supplies the comparison.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ˈlaŋzaːmɐ]: the stressed [a] is short; the second syllable has long [aː], and the comparative ending is vocalized [ɐ]. Langsamer can carry the comparison accent.

common.sentence: Die Stadt prüft erst die Zufahrt, dann die Beleuchtung.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of prüft; erst and dann establish the order.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [diː ˈt͡suːfaːɐ̯t]: the article and the stressed [uː] are long and close; Zufahrt can be prominent as the first item in the sequence.

common.sentence: Ben liest die Überschrift vor, Lea anschließend den ersten Absatz.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of the understood liest vor; ersten has weak -en after den.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [deːn ˈʔeːɐ̯stən ˈʔapzat͡s]: ersten has long close-mid [eː]; Absatz has short [a] and final [t͡s]. Absatz can be prominent against Überschrift.

common.sentence: Mara meldet einen vorläufigen Wert; die endgültige Zahl fehlt noch.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of meldet; vorläufigen has mixed -en after einen.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ˈfoːɐ̯lɔʏ̯fɪɡən veːɐ̯t]: vorläufigen contains [ɔʏ̯]; Wert has long close-mid [eː]. Vorläufigen can be prominent against endgültige.

common.sentence: Lea probt die Oberstimme, Ben dagegen die Bassstimme.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of probt; probt is understood in the second clause.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ˈoːbɐˌʃtɪmə]: primary word stress falls on long close-mid [oː]; Stimme has short lax [ɪ] and final schwa. Oberstimme can carry contrastive sentence prominence against Bassstimme.

common.sentence: Nach der Begehung erläutert Mara dem Ausschuss die nächsten Schritte.

language_specific.grammar: Nach governs dative singular der Begehung; the fronted phrase specifies when Mara explains the steps.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [naːx deːɐ̯ bəˈɡeːʊŋ]: nach has long [aː], and Begehung has stressed long close-mid [eː]. A phrase boundary may follow Begehung without an obligatory pause.

common.sentence: Der Chor, heute ohne Klavier, beginnt mit einem Volkslied.

language_specific.grammar: Ohne governs accusative singular Klavier; the inserted phrase describes today's accompaniment.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ˈhɔʏ̯tə ˈoːnə klaˈviːɐ̯]: heute has [ɔʏ̯], ohne long close-mid [oː], and Klavier stressed long close [iː]. Boundaries can set off the insertion.

common.sentence: Bei Starkregen kann Wasser über den Weg in die Mulde fließen.

language_specific.grammar: Bei governs dative singular Starkregen; the fronted phrase states the condition under which the described flow is possible.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [baɪ̯ ˈʃtaʁkˌʁeːɡən]: bei has [aɪ̯]; Stark has short [a], and Regen has long close-mid [eː]. A phrase boundary may follow Starkregen, grouping the condition before the main clause; an audible pause is optional.

common.sentence: Sobald die Gäste sitzen, begrüßt Ben sie im Namen des Chors.
common.meaning: as soon as the guests are seated

language_specific.grammar: The fronted sobald clause has plural Gäste as subject and clause-final sitzen; begrüßt follows in the main clause.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [zoˈbalt diː ˈɡɛstə ˈzɪt͡sən]: sobald has stressed short [a], Gäste short open-mid [ɛ], and sitzen short lax [ɪ]. A boundary may follow sitzen.

common.sentence: Die Weide am Bach, nicht die am Weg, bleibt stehen.
common.meaning: not the one by the path

language_specific.grammar: Die refers back to Weide; am contracts an dem and marks location with dative Weg.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [nɪçt diː ʔam veːk]: nicht has short lax [ɪ], and Weg has long close-mid [eː] and final [k]. Boundaries can set off the correction; Weg can be prominent against Bach.

common.sentence: Lea, die heute moderiert, stellt Ben vor dem ersten Lied vor.

language_specific.grammar: Die refers to Lea and is the nominative subject; moderiert is clause-final.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [diː ˈhɔʏ̯tə modeˈʁiːɐ̯t]: heute has [ɔʏ̯]; moderiert has stressed long close [iː] followed by vocalized r. Boundaries can set off the relative clause.

common.sentence: Mara fragt: „Reicht das Budget für die Pflege der Hecke?“

language_specific.grammar: Reicht is the first-position finite verb; das Budget is its nominative subject and für introduces the purpose.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ʁaɪ̯çt das bʏˈdʒeː]: reicht has [aɪ̯]; Budget has final stress on long close-mid [eː]. The complete yes-no question may have rising final pitch; the written text does not fix its contour.

common.sentence: Ben fragt Lea: „Welches Lied eröffnet heute das Konzert?“

language_specific.grammar: Welches Lied is the nominative subject of eröffnet; das Konzert is the accusative object.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ˈvɛlçəs liːt]: welches has short open-mid [ɛ], and Lied has long close [iː] and final [t]. A falling contour is one possible way to complete the full question.

common.sentence: Mara markiert für ihren Vortrag den Wortakzent in „Versickerung“.

language_specific.grammar: Accusative singular object of markiert; in „Versickerung“ identifies the word whose stress is marked.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [ˈvɔʁtʔakˌt͡sɛnt]: primary stress falls on Wort, with short open-mid [ɔ]; Akzent has short [a] and short open-mid [ɛ]. In the named word Versickerung [fɛɐ̯ˈzɪkəʁʊŋ], primary stress falls on the short lax [ɪ] of the second syllable.

common.sentence: Lea sagt zum Chor: „Nach dem Lied folgt eine kurze Pause.“

language_specific.grammar: Nach governs dative singular dem Lied; the fronted phrase gives the time of the pause.
language_specific.pronunciation: Target [naːx deːm liːt]: nach has long [aː]; dem has long close-mid [eː] and Lied has long close [iː], and Lied ends in [t]. A boundary may follow Lied to group the time phrase; a pause is optional.
